anchors.fact: Norman Hobday (1933-2011) opened Henry Africa's in San Francisco in 1969 (Oxford pdf 995; *Proper* p. 51: Broadway and Polk; he "helped kick off the fern bar movement"). F1, F2, F22; A7
anchors.meaning: The one who changed the room. Never "the first fern bar" (C1: the Trident was three years earlier).

anchors.fact: By his own account (Chronicle 2011), when he found the place it was a bar with blackened windows. F13; A8
anchors.meaning: The old room as it was. Told as his account. Never say he changed the windows.

anchors.fact: "There wasn't enough money to remodel", so he brought in plants: they "did a hell of a job for what they cost" (Chronicle 2011, his words). F14; A9
anchors.meaning: The sensible reason, said out loud. On the record, so the bartender grants it ("I believe him").
anchors.speaksTo: the practical argument that hides the love

anchors.fact: "It was bright and cheery. People started swarming in there" (Chronicle 2011). Fern bars made barrooms bright places where "both sexes could mingle on equal terms" (Oxford pdf 770). F6, F15; A2, A10
anchors.meaning: More people let in. Women on equal terms is the story's change, never a point about the guest.
anchors.speaksTo: more people in the shared place

anchors.fact: Many singles bars were dressed like 1890s Gilded Age lounges ("brass rails, Tiffany lamps, and potted plants"), lounges that "had often banned unescorted women"; the change was made by "nostalgists" as well as feminists and ecologists (Oxford pdf 995, 770). F4, F5, F7; A3, A4
anchors.meaning: The old look brought back, holding everyone. It's a look revived ("fancifully resurrected"), not furniture kept, and the movement's nostalgia isn't Hobday's stated motive.
anchors.speaksTo: the old form kept, the welcome changed

anchors.fact: Hobday "loved his bar as much as his customers did", legally took its name, Henry Africa, a few years before it closed, and kept it until he died (Oxford pdf 995; Chronicle 2011). F12, F17; A11
anchors.meaning: The love shows in staying, not in what he said. "I like to think it was never the whole reason" is the one signposted sentence. Dossier only: in his telling the name came from his mother's condition (F16).

anchors.fact: Fern bars are credited with bringing the American saloon back from the dead (Oxford pdf 770, paraphrased; never its eight-word run). F8; A5
anchors.meaning: The change saved the old thing.

anchors.fact: Henry Africa's closed in 1986 (Oxford pdf 995). By the early 2000s, the craft movement's principles included keeping "the gender-inclusive bars" and the women behind the bar (Oxford pdf 1332). F10, F11; A6, A13
anchors.meaning: The bar closed and the change didn't. The movement was "people", drinkers and bartenders together, not "a new generation of bartenders".

anchors.fact: The Lemon Drop, Hobday's "most enduring original cocktail" (Oxford pdf 995); the original was "a more elegant affair", served up in a sugar-rimmed cocktail glass, before it became a shot. His bar used fresh juices to order (pdf 1175). F18-F20; A14-A16
anchors.meaning: Made the elegant way it began. Never "his recipe" (C2: *Proper* p. 52 adds triple sec) and never "his lemon" (C3). The ratio and the outside-only rim all the way round are ours. No "mask".

anchors.fact: James C. Maloney's *20th Century Guide for Mixing Fancy Drinks* (Chicago, 1900) prints a family of Bell-Ringers whose glass is coated inside with "Eagle Creme D'Apricot" ("abricotine"), red, before the drink goes in; half a teaspoon in the Gin and Manhattan ones; also in the *Police Gazette* 1902-03. B1-B7; A17
anchors.meaning: The old era's gesture around the new drink. Date: "1900", never "1890s" (C6); "close to" or "at the very end of" the era the fern bars dressed up as. His was a sweet red liqueur. "Tip nothing out" is ours (B2).
anchors.speaksTo: the old form kept, holding the new

anchors.fact: Dry apricot eau-de-vie in place of his liqueur: "less sweet and more delicate" (Oxford pdf 133, "little residual sugar"). Apricot pairs with citrus and fruit brandy (*Flavor Matrix* pdf 236, rendered). B8; A18
anchors.meaning: Our swap, said as ours: the glass smells of apricot without being any sweeter. Veto-free under Robin's evidence rule (2026-10-06): no page names kernels in the eau-de-vie (Oxford pdf 133: apricots and pomace).

cocktail.closingLine: Coat the glass before you pour. And before you change anything, say what you're keeping.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail coupe (about 200 ml), chilled, coated inside with apricot eau-de-vie, fine sugar on the outside of the rim
method: Put the coupe in the freezer for ten minutes.
Pour the half teaspoon of apricot eau-de-vie into a saucer, and spread a little fine sugar on a second saucer.
Turn the cold glass upside down and roll the outside edge of its rim through the apricot spirit, then through the sugar, until a thin band of sugar runs all the way round the outside.
Pour what's left of the apricot spirit into the glass and turn the glass slowly until the inside is coated. Leave it there. Nothing gets tipped out.
Put the vodka, lemon juice and simple syrup in a shaker, fill it with ice and shake hard for 10 to 15 seconds.
cocktail.name: Not the Same

recipe.note: any plain, unflavoured vodka of 40% or stronger; not a citrus vodka
one part sugar dissolved in one part warm water, cooled

a clear, dry apricot brandy (Hungarian barack pálinka or Austrian Marillenbrand style), not the sweet apricot-flavoured kind. It coats the glass, the way a Chicago bartender coated his glasses in 1900
on the outside of the rim only

cocktail.tagline: People think you want to change it. You're the one who loves it most.

reading.epigraph: A Chicago bar guide of 1900 says to coat the glass. The drink came decades later.
whoYouAre: Every summer there's the same street party, and every summer a few more people find a reason to miss it. You're the one who suggests the Saturday instead of the Sunday, and the neighbours nobody ever thought to knock for. You keep the food everyone brings, the old songs, the raffle with the terrible prizes. Someone who's been coming for thirty years tells you it won't be the same. It isn't. The next summer, the street is full.

Here's the part nobody guesses: you love the old version more than the people defending it. You argue with dates and numbers, because "I'd hate to lose this" sounds soft, so the ones who love it too can hear someone wrecking it. The row doesn't scare you. What does is the change you pushed for turning out to be what finishes it off, and everyone remembering it was you. And look what you leave instead: the things people love are still there, with more people in them, because someone cared enough to change them. Nobody says so at the time. Someone should.
yours: Before he opened Henry Africa's in San Francisco in 1969, Norman Hobday found the place, which he remembered as a bar with blackened windows. There wasn't enough money to remodel, he said later, so he brought in plants. As he put it, they did "a hell of a job for what they cost". It was bright and cheery, he said, and people started swarming in.

Hobday loved the place as much as his customers did. A few years before it closed, he legally changed his own name to the bar's, Henry Africa, and kept it until he died. Many bars like his were done up with brass, Tiffany lamps and ferns, like the lounges of the 1890s, which had often turned away women who came on their own. Now women and men came in on equal terms. Fern bars are credited with bringing the American saloon back from the dead.

He gave the cheap reason, and I believe him. But I like to think it was never the whole reason: nobody takes a bar's name for the rest of their life over a cheap fix. You'd know that move. You give the sensible reason out loud, and the love shows in how long you stay. And what you change tends to outlive the place. Henry Africa's closed in 1986. The change didn't. When the bar world went back to the old craft in the early 2000s, it chose to keep, among other things, the bars where women drank on equal terms, and the women working behind them.

The cocktail I've made for you is Hobday's most enduring drink, the Lemon Drop, made the elegant way it was first served, before it shrank into a shot: up, in a sugar-rimmed glass. Mine is a chilled coupe, and I take the sugar all the way round. The lemon is squeezed fresh, the way his bar made its juices, to order. It tastes of the lemon candy it's named after, sweet and bright. The change is in the glass. In a Chicago bar guide from 1900, James Maloney gave a set of drinks that went into a glass coated inside with apricot liqueur, a sweet red one. I do the same with a clear, dry apricot brandy. Half a teaspoon is enough to coat the glass and hold the rim's sugar in place, and I tip none of it out. It's there as a nod to what you do: the old thing kept on purpose, holding the new one. The apricot reaches you first, then the lemon.

One thing I'd like you to try. You keep the love behind the sensible reasons, and that's why the people defending the old version hear an enemy. Let them hear the love first, before the dates and the numbers. They'll find someone on their side, because you always were. And once the place is full again, don't stand by the wall checking that it held. Go in and enjoy it. It was always as much yours as theirs.
